Article Title: Tilak Varma in India’s ODI World Cup plans as selectors seek Shreyas Iyer backup
Article Text:
India's Shreyas Iyer, center, with batting partner Tilak Varma (AP/PTI)

Selectors wary of moving batters around

Team for Afg series likely by Sept 3

New Delhi: India’s team management and selectors are working on backups for the middle order ahead of the ODI World Cup next year. TOI has learnt that Tilak Varma’s name has come up as a potential backup option for Shreyas Iyer in the top six of the batting lineup.Tilak, being a left-handed batter, is seen as someone who can break the monotony of right-handers in the batting lineup. Tilak has been asked to work on his bowling since it is believed that his off-breaks have a lot of potential. The team management, in fact, has flagged the dearth of bowling options in the top order, citing it as a reason for extra pressure on the lower order and the bowlers.The planning for the ODI World Cup will only begin in earnest when India reach New Zealand in October, since most of the first-choice players will not be available for the ODI series against West Indies at home from September 27. A full-strength T20 team is also scheduled to travel to Japan for the Asian Games at the same time.“Head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Shubman Gill feel there isn’t any backup ready for the middle order. With Hardik Pandya and Nitish Kumar Reddy being prone to injuries, they want someone in the top order who can at least chip in with four overs in an ODI,” a BCCI source said.Over the last year, the team management has been compelled to play either Washington Sundar or Axar Patel at No.5 or No. 6 to balance the playing XI. In the last series in England, Ishan Kishan was sent in ahead of vice-captain Iyer.“The team has to be prepared for conditions in South Africa in the World Cup. Iyer got injured in Australia and his game against pace and bounce is untested of late. The team already has two ageing players in Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli. They are having niggles as well. KL Rahul too will be over 35 by the time the World Cup comes around. Ravindra Jadeja isn’t a certainty either. The fielding of the team has suffered due to fitness issues. The team management feels that they need younger backups ready,” the source said.The selectors, it is learnt, are not comfortable with playing batters out of position. Last year, Ruturaj Gaikwad was played at No. 4 and scored a hundred against South Africa in Raipur. But he has not been picked in the ODI team since.“Gaikwad was picked as backup opener since Gill was injured. The team management feels Tilak could have been tried in that place. That’s why they don’t want to rush Devdutt Padikkal in the ODI setup because he found his calling in white-ball cricket while opening the batting,” the source said.The team for the West Indies series, however, will be an anomaly since Iyer, Tilak, Ishan and Axar will not be available. The selectors are more focused on picking another wicketkeeper for the series.The selection committee is due to meet by September 3 to pick the team for the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan in Delhi from September 13.Sources said that the selectors are likely to retain the team selected for the subsequent Asian Games. The official fitness reports of Hardik, Nitish Reddy and Jasprit Bumrah are awaited. Varun Chakravarthy has regained full fitness, it is learnt.
Article Summary: Tilak varma’s name has come up as a potential backup option for shreyas iyer. Tilak has been asked to work on his bowling since it is believed that his off-breaks have a lot of potential. Most of the first-choice players will not be available for the odi series against west indies at home from september 27.

Sriram Kartik sweeps 10 awards including the ‘Best Junior contestant’ across Carnatic vocal and mrudangam; prizes presented by eminent Vidwan Sikkil Gurucharan on 23 Aug 2026 in MumbaiA fifteen-year-old from Powai has won ten awards at the Music Competition 2026 conducted by Sri Shanmukhananda Bharatiya Sangeetha Vidyalaya and Natya Vidyalaya, competing in both Carnatic vocal and mrudangam.Sriram Kartik, a Class X IGCSE student at Podar International School, received the awards at the prize distribution ceremony held on Sunday (Aug 23, 2026) on the occasion of Shanmukhananda's Carnataka Sangeetha Pon Mazhai Thiruvizha, at the Sri Shanmukhananda Fine Arts and Sangeetha Sabha in Matunga. The prizes were presented by Shanmukha Sangeetha Shiromani Vidwan Shri Sikkil Gurucharan, the eminent Carnatic vocalist, who presided over the ceremony.Vidwan Sikkil C Gurucharan is a leading Indian Carnatic classical vocalist and youth ambassador for the art form. A singer born into a family of flautists, and grandson of Sikkil Kunjumani, the elder of the Sikkil Sisters, he trained under B Krishnamurthy and Vaigal S. Gnanaskandan, himself a disciple of Semmangudi Srinivasa Iyer and gave his first concert at The Music Academy, Chennai at the age of twelve. Recipient of the Kalaimamani award from the Tamil Nadu government in 2020, Sikkil C Gurucharan has been featured by India Today as one of the 35 Game Changers Under 35 in India.Sriram Kartik won 9 individual prizes — five first prizes, three seconds and one third. He was also awarded a cash prize for being the Best Junior contestant winning the maximum number of prizes in the 10-to-15 years age category.The competition, the Vidyalaya's 70th annual, was held on February 7 and 8 across Carnatic vocal, violin, veena, mrudangam, Hindustani vocal, sitar and tabla. It drew more than 300 participants from across India and overseas, contesting in three age groups: 10 to 15, 16 to 28, and 29 and above.Sriram's two mrudangam prizes came in the only two categories open to his age group — a first for tani avartanam in roopakam and misra chapu talams, and a second for adi talam with five jathi mohras, awarded under the TS Nandakumar's Percussive Arts Centre Endowment and the Guru TS Nandakumar Endowment respectively.His seven vocal prizes spanned first places in compositions of the Trinity, varnams, Purandaradasa kritis; the Silver Lamp Prize for keertanams and kritis; second places in Subramania Bharatiyar compositions and Tamizh compositions; and a third in GNB kritis.Every prize at Shanmukhananda is attached to an endowment instituted in the name of an artist, a patron or an institution. He won awards under the following endowments namely - GNB Endowment, the Kalki Memorial, the Dr S Pinakapani Endowment, the BVS Iyengar Memorial and the Lakshmi Gopalakrishna Memorial. The Best Junior award came under the Smt. Parvathy Subramaniam Endowment and S Ramakrishnan Memorial.Sriram began learning the mrudangam at the age of five, under Acharya Ratna Vidwan Mumbai Shri Shankaranarayanan at Powai Fine Arts. A decade on, he has kept at it through the school years in which most students of classical music quietly stop — the age at which coaching classes, board examinations and the ordinary pull of everything else tend to close the practice room door for good.Sustaining it alongside school is the part a prize list does not show. Practice sessions run two and a half to three hours. Nine vocal categories at 5-6 compositions a piece meant something close to 45-50 pieces in which he participated of which he won prizes across seven categories, readied to a standard that would survive a judging panel, with two percussion categories besides.He now receives higher tutelage in mrudangam from Padma Vibhushan and Sangeet Natak Academi Awardee Vidwan Dr Umayalpuram K Sivaraman, and trains in Carnatic vocal music under Acharya Ratnakara Vidwan Sherthalai Dr KN Renganatha Sharma and Vidushi Dr Mohana Sharma. He holds a CCRT Scholarship for Mrudangam from the ministry of culture, and presented his mrudangam arangetram in June last year, the day after his fourteenth birthday.

The competition drew more than 300 participants from across india and overseas, contesting in three age groups: 10 to 15, 16 to 28, and 29 and above.

Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “My dad had four jobs at one time just to keep me karting” - How Lewis Hamilton and his father turned second-hand kart, and family sacrifice into F1 immortality
Article Text:
Inspiring story of the day: “My dad had four jobs at one time just to keep me karting” - How Lewis Hamilton and his father turned second-hand kart, and family sacrifice into F1 immortality

How did Anthony Hamilton help Lewis Hamilton start his karting career

What did Lewis Hamilton learn from his father about racism and racing

Why did Lewis Hamilton and Anthony Hamilton stop working together

How did Lewis Hamilton’s family sacrifice connect to his seven F1 titles

Lewis Hamilton’s Formula 1 success did not start with fame, money or a big racing team. It began when he was a child in Stevenage, with his father Anthony Hamilton doing whatever he could to keep his son’s karting dream alive. Anthony worked several jobs while also acting as Lewis’s mechanic and helping him travel to races. Hamilton has said his father’s work ethic and advice stayed with him as he moved into Formula 1. Their professional relationship later became difficult, but the two eventually rebuilt their bond. The story behind Hamilton’s rise remains closely tied to the sacrifices his family made.Lewis Hamilton was eight when his father began managing his racing career, and Anthony quickly became much more than a parent watching from the sidelines. He helped prepare the kart, travelled with Lewis and worked to find the money needed to keep him racing.In a 2023 interview discussed by PlanetF1, Hamilton explained just how much his father was doing at the time. “My dad had four jobs at one stage just to keep us go-karting because, when we started karting, the majority of the people were from working-class families,” Hamilton said.That early life was very hands-on. Hamilton also explained that Anthony was his mechanic and that the family travelled together for race weekends.His stepmother, Linda, helped make sure the family had what they needed while they were on the road.Anthony’s role was not simply about finding money. He was also learning how to work on the kart and helping Lewis compete against drivers who had greater access to equipment and mechanics. That experience gave Hamilton an early understanding of how much work went into staying in racing.The sacrifice was especially important because karting can be expensive, and young drivers need regular races and equipment to keep progressing. Anthony did not have the resources of wealthy families in the sport, so the family had to make the opportunity work with what they had.Hamilton also grew up dealing with racism and bullying while competing in motorsport. He has spoken about being the only Black family at some racing events and about being made to feel that he did not belong.His father’s response became one of the most important lessons in Hamilton’s career.In an interview with BBC Sport, Hamilton said: “It’s just how my dad raised me. He said to always do your talking on the track.”The advice was simple: do not waste energy trying to answer people with words. Prove yourself through your driving.Hamilton has described being bullied both at school and on the karting circuit. Instead of allowing those experiences to take him away from racing, he used them as motivation to become better.That mindset followed him into Formula 1. Even after reaching the sport’s biggest stage, Hamilton continued to speak about letting his results answer his critics.His father’s influence was therefore not limited to the practical side of racing. Anthony helped shape the attitude Lewis carried into a career where he would face pressure, criticism and scrutiny at almost every stage.The father-son partnership changed once Lewis reached Formula 1. Anthony managed his son through his early years in the sport, including Hamilton’s breakthrough with McLaren and his first world championship in 2008.But in 2010, Lewis decided that his father should no longer manage his professional career.Hamilton was 25 at the time and said the change was needed so the two could have a healthier relationship away from business. The decision did not mean Anthony stopped being important to him. In fact, Hamilton said he wanted his father to simply be his dad.Autosport reported the management change in 2010 after speaking exclusively with Hamilton. He explained that he wanted someone else to handle the professional side while he and his father could focus on their family relationship.The split was not completely easy. The Guardian reported that the two did not speak for several weeks after the professional separation. Hamilton later acknowledged that their relationship had gone through a difficult period.By 2020, however, Hamilton spoke openly about how they had worked to rebuild their bond. BBC Sport reported that he described their journey as difficult and said they had both wanted their father-son relationship back.That part of the story matters because Anthony’s role in Hamilton’s career was never only about management. For years, he had been his father, mechanic, mentor and guide at the same time.Hamilton’s first Formula 1 world title came in 2008, only a year after he made his F1 debut. Twelve years later, he matched Michael Schumacher’s record of seven world championships by winning the 2020 Turkish Grand Prix.Formula 1 reported that Hamilton became emotional after securing the seventh title, saying the scale of the achievement had caused him to “burst into tears.”The result was the biggest sporting reward yet for a journey that had started with his father working multiple jobs to keep him karting.Hamilton’s rise also carried wider importance. He became the first Black driver to compete in Formula 1 and went on to become one of the sport’s most successful drivers. His early experiences with his father helped shape the way he approached both racing and the barriers around it.The story is not simply about a young driver becoming a champion. It is also about the years of work that came before the trophies, contracts and global attention.Anthony Hamilton helped Lewis reach the starting line when the path ahead was far from certain. Lewis then turned that opportunity into one of the greatest careers Formula 1 has seen. Their journey included success, pressure, a difficult professional split and, eventually, a stronger focus on being father and son.For Hamilton, the lessons from those early karting years never disappeared. His father’s work ethic and one simple instruction - “Do your talking on the track” - became part of the way he approached racing and the challenges that came with it.

It began when he was a child in stevenage, with his father anthony hamilton doing whatever he could to keep his son's karting dream alive. Article Title: 'Pakistan chapter I had before is now closed': Mohammad Amir calls himself 'British local'
Article Text:
Mohammad Amir. (File Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A career remembered for big moments

Mohammad Amir has ended speculation over a possible return to Pakistan's national team, confirming that his international career is now firmly behind him.The left-arm pacer, who retired from international cricket in December 2024, has obtained British citizenship and a British passport through his wife, Narjis Khan.Amir explained that his new status means he can no longer be treated as a local Pakistani player in competitions such as the County Championship and The Hundred. Players registered as locals in English domestic cricket must declare that they will not represent another country as a local player."I am a British local now. When you play in competitions such as the County Championship and The Hundred as a local player, you have to sign a document stating that you cannot play for another country as a local. So, the Pakistan chapter I had before is now closed," Amir said in an interview with cricket YouTuber Furqan Bhatti.Amir represented Pakistan in 36 Tests, 61 ODIs and 62 T20Is, taking 119, 81 and 71 wickets respectively. He also played in three World Cups, including the 2019 ODI World Cup, where he was Pakistan's leading wicket-taker with 17 wickets.Amir played important roles in Pakistan's 2009 T20 World Cup and 2017 Champions Trophy triumphs.His most memorable performance came in the 2017 Champions Trophy final against India, where he took 3-16 and dismissed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shikhar Dhawan. Pakistan went on to win by 180 runs.He also impressed at the 2019 World Cup, taking a five-wicket haul against Australia.While his decision may disappoint supporters who hoped to see him return for the 2027 World Cup, Amir's international career already includes several unforgettable performances. His move to British citizenship allows him to extend his career in county and franchise cricket, while his achievements for Pakistan remain a major part of his legacy.
Article Summary: Mohammad amir has retired from international cricket in december 2024. The left-arm pacer has obtained british citizenship and a british passport through his wife, narjis khan. His new status means he can no longer be treated as a local pakistani player in competitions such as the county championship and the hundred.

Bengaluru: The 2026-27 domestic season is barely underway, but the old North-South rivalry is already adding spice to the Duleep Trophy. North Zone and South Zone will renew their contest in the semifinals at the BCCI Centre of Excellence here from Sunday, with youth and experience on both sides making for an intriguing battle.North bring the exuberance of youth, with the likes of Ayush Doseja keen to build on early promise. South, runners-up in the last edition, have a blend of emerging talent and established names, with Karnataka youngster R Smaran joining the likes of Tilak Varma and Karun Nair.On paper, the contest could boil down to South’s formidable batting against North’s in-form bowling. Smaran, the leading run-scorer in last season’s Ranji Trophy with 950 runs, will be one of South’s key batters, while captain Tilak, Karun and Narayan Jagadeesan give the side considerable depth.When the two sides met in the previous edition, South had the upper hand, with Jagadeesan’s 197 helping them secure a sizeable first-innings lead before they eventually marched into the final.This time, however, South will have to contend with a North attack brimming with confidence. Left-arm spinner Abid Mushtaq was instrumental in their quarterfinal win over West Zone, claiming nine wickets. If the surface offers turn, Mushtaq and Nishant Sindhu could pose a serious challenge to South’s batting.For East Zone’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the other semifinal against defending champions Central Zone offers another opportunity to make a statement in red-ball cricket.The 15-year-old southpaw managed a single-digit score against Northeast Zone in the quarterfinal and will be eager to make a bigger contribution this time. Central, meanwhile, will be led by Rajat Patidar, setting up another strategic test for Sooryavanshi.

Article Title: Players at the US Open in New York are complaining that the smell of marijuana is becoming an unwanted distraction
Article Text:
Players at the US Open in New York say marijuana smoke is becoming an unexpected distraction/ Photo by Dave Dellinger/USTA

Boulter: ‘You don't need distractions’

Jones remembers the smell from last year's US Open

It has been an issue at the US Open before

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The 2026 US Open is set to begin on Sunday, but as the world's best players prepare for the year's final Grand Slam, some competitors are dealing with an unexpected distraction around Flushing Meadows: the smell of cannabis drifting in from a nearby park.British players Katie Boulter, Fran Jones and Harriet Dart have all noticed the smell around the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, with Boulter saying it can affect her concentration during practice and matches.The tournament begins on Aug. 30, with Carlos Alcaraz returning to individual competition for the first time since suffering a wrist injury at the Barcelona Open in April. World No. 1 Jannik Sinner will miss the event with a knee injury, while Novak Djokovic will pursue a record 25th Grand Slam title. Rising star Alex Eala is also expected to receive strong support from New York fans, while Aryna Sabalenka will look to rediscover her best form.Cannabis is legal for adults aged 21 and over in New York, although smoking is not permitted on the grounds of the tennis center. However, the venue sits beside Corona Park, and the smell can carry across to some practice and outside courts.Boulter, Britain's No. 1 and ranked 60th in the world, said she has encountered it both while practising and during matches.“Yeah, I have experienced it. You go down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot,” Boulter said.“But yeah, I'm not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on some of the specific courts.“I've played on one before and I did smell it during my match. It's something that I wouldn't like to smell in the middle of my match.“I'm trying to focus and then obviously, it takes you out of the moment and you really don't want to. You don't need distractions. So yeah, I wasn't a huge fan of it.”Boulter is not the only British player to have noticed it. Fran Jones, Britain's No. 3, recalled encountering the smell during her first-round match at last year's tournament and said she initially wondered whether it was simply part of playing so close to the park.“Last year I made a joke about that, in my first round, and I said to the guy, 'is this normal?' Because I was on the stadium, and it's next to the park,” Jones said.“He's like, 'yeah.' and I was like, 'well, no wonder I'm playing pretty well.'“This year I'll be like 'no, lock in, lock in!'”Jones, who qualified for this year's tournament, begins her campaign against Poland's Magda Linette on Monday.Harriet Dart, who also came through qualifying, took a more typically New York approach to the situation.“I mean it's New York. It's New York. I feel like everywhere you walk around, it's everywhere, no? It is what it is. Same for everyone,” Dart said.Dart will face American Peyton Stearns in the first round.The smell of cannabis has become a recurring talking point at Flushing Meadows, with players from outside Britain raising similar concerns in previous editions.In 2022, Australian doubles player Nick Kyrgios complained that a spectator smoking courtside was affecting his asthma, prompting the umpire to ask fans to refrain from smoking.A year later, Greece's Maria Sakkari pointed out the smell to the umpire during a match. She later clarified that it was not an excuse for her defeat.Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev have also previously noticed the smell around the tournament.The United States Tennis Association, which organises the US Open, has acknowledged the difficulty of dealing with activity taking place beyond the tournament grounds.“While we can't control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this,” the USTA said in a statement.The organisation has said it works with local police and the parks department to address smoking around the boundary of the site.With the 2026 US Open getting under way on Sunday, the cannabis smell is likely to remain a background issue at a tournament already filled with major storylines. Alcaraz will return to action, Sinner will be absent, Djokovic will chase another historic title, Eala will look to make the most of strong local support and Sabalenka will aim to regain her winning form.Boulter will open against American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee, while Jones and Dart begin their campaigns against Linette and Stearns respectively.
Article Summary: Players at the us open in new york say marijuana smoke is becoming an unexpected distraction. Katie boulter, fran jones and harriet dart have all noticed the smell around the usta billie jean king national tennis center. The 2026 us open is set to begin on sunday.

Article Title: Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family
Article Text:
Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family

What did Andre Agassi mean when he said, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood”?

How did becoming a father change Agassi’s view of his own childhood?

How did Steffi Graf fit into Agassi’s approach to raising their children?

What does Agassi’s quote tell us about his idea of parenthood?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Andre Agassi’s words, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” offer a deeply personal look at how becoming a parent changed the tennis legend’s view of his own life. Agassi grew up in a world where tennis was not simply a sport but a major part of his everyday life, with intense training and expectations starting at a very young age. Years later, after becoming one of tennis’ biggest stars, he and his wife, fellow tennis legend Steffi Graf, built a family life around their two children, Jaden and Jaz. For Agassi, watching his children grow gave him the chance to experience some of the simple moments of childhood that he felt he had missed himself.The quote is closely connected to Agassi’s own experience growing up. He started playing tennis as a young child and was pushed toward the sport by his father, Mike Agassi. His father had a clear dream for him: he wanted his son to become one of the best tennis players in the world.That dream eventually came true.Agassi went on to become world No. 1 and won eight Grand Slam singles titles during his career. But reaching that level meant spending much of his childhood training, competing and preparing for professional tennis.For a young child, that kind of life can leave little room for ordinary experiences. Instead of having complete freedom to decide how he wanted to spend his time, Agassi’s days were largely connected to tennis.That is where his famous quote becomes especially powerful.When he says he “gave up” his childhood, he is looking back at the years he spent becoming a professional athlete. But he is also talking about what those sacrifices eventually allowed him to do.His success gave him the freedom to step away from tennis and spend more time with his family. It allowed him to be present as his children grew up.In other words, Agassi may have missed parts of his own childhood, but later he had the opportunity to sit beside his children and watch them experience theirs. For him, that became a kind of second chance.Fatherhood gave Agassi a different way of looking at his past. When he watched Jaden and Jaz grow up, he could see the small moments of childhood from a parent’s point of view.He could watch them discover what they liked, make their own choices and develop personalities separate from their famous parents.Those moments were very different from the childhood Agassi had experienced.His early years were strongly connected to the tennis court. His father believed that constant practice and discipline were necessary if Agassi was going to become a champion. That approach helped produce an incredible tennis career, but it also meant that Agassi’s childhood was far from ordinary.As a father, he wanted something different for his children.Instead of seeing childhood as preparation for a future career, Agassi wanted Jaden and Jaz to enjoy the years they were living through.That is one of the most important ideas behind his quote. He was not simply saying that he wanted to give his children more material things or better opportunities. He wanted to give them time.Time to grow.Time to explore.Time to make mistakes.Time to decide what they wanted for themselves.This became especially important because Agassi knew from personal experience how powerful parental expectations can be. He had spent years trying to become the player his father wanted him to be. As a parent, he had the chance to make sure his own children did not feel that same pressure.Steffi Graf’s role in the family’s story is important because she understood Agassi’s world better than almost anyone. Like her husband, Graf was introduced to tennis at a very young age and went on to become one of the greatest players in the history of the sport.Graf won 22 Grand Slam singles titles and spent years at the top of women’s tennis before retiring in 1999. Agassi and Graf later married and raised their two children, Jaden and Jaz.Together, they had something unusual in common: both parents knew exactly what it took to become a tennis champion, but they also knew the pressure that came with that journey.That understanding appears to have influenced the way they raised their children.Despite having two parents who were global tennis stars, Jaden and Jaz were not simply expected to follow the same path.Jaden developed a passion for baseball rather than choosing tennis as his main sport. Jaz has also been able to follow her own interests. Agassi and Graf have supported their children without making their parents’ careers the center of their lives.That is particularly meaningful when viewed alongside Agassi’s quote.The couple had already achieved what many athletes spend their entire lives chasing. They did not need their children to continue that legacy for them.Instead, they could give their children something that both parents understood the value of: choice.Agassi has also spoken warmly about Graf and the role she plays in his life. Their shared experience in professional sports gave them an understanding of the demands and sacrifices that come with elite competition.For their family, giving their children the freedom to choose their own paths became more important than creating another generation of tennis champions.At its heart, Agassi’s quote is about turning his own difficult experiences into something positive for his children.He cannot go back and change the childhood he had. He cannot erase the years of training, pressure and expectations that came with becoming a tennis player.But he can choose what kind of childhood his own children experience.That is what makes the quote about much more than tennis.Many parents work hard because they want their children to have opportunities they did not have themselves. Agassi’s story takes that idea one step further. His goal was not simply to provide his children with a comfortable life. He wanted to be present for the experiences that make childhood special.His words also show that parenthood can change the way people understand their own past.The same childhood that once felt difficult to Agassi became part of what helped him understand his children better. His experiences taught him what pressure can feel like, which may have made him more aware of the importance of giving his own children freedom.And Steffi Graf was there beside him, bringing her own experience as a former champion and a parent.Together, Agassi and Graf chose not to make their children’s lives about living up to their parents’ names. They allowed Jaden and Jaz to build identities of their own.That may be the most powerful part of Agassi’s words.He spent his childhood becoming a tennis champion. But when he became a father, he did not want his children to spend their childhood becoming something for him.He wanted to watch them simply be children.So, when Agassi says, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” he is not only talking about sacrifice. He is talking about perspective, presence and love.He gave years of his life to tennis. Those years helped him become a champion and eventually gave him the freedom to step back and focus on his family.For Agassi, one of the greatest rewards was not another trophy or achievement. It was being able to watch his children grow up on their own terms, with Graf by his side.That is what makes his quote so relatable. Parenthood does not allow us to rewrite our own childhoods, but it can give us the chance to create a different childhood for the next generation.
Article Summary: Andre agassi’s famous quote is closely connected to his own experience growing up. Agassi spent much of his childhood training, competing and preparing for professional tennis. His success gave him the freedom to step away from tennis and spend more time with his family.

Article Title: ‘CoE cannot be only for contracted players’: VVS Laxman on building India’s cricket pipeline
Article Text:
VVS Laxman

From a compact facility at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium to the expansive centre, how has the journey been?

What, according to you, has been the biggest change?

While contracted players benefit from the facility, how has it been working with domestic players, giving them more access to technology, quality coaching, and support staff?

Active players have now started taking a keen interest in coaching and are going through the coaching courses. What do you attribute this trend to?

Can you put down in numbers the high performance camps that CoE conducts across the country in a year?

The setting up of the women’s coaching system -- what’s that process been like?

VVS Laxman with women's cricketers

How much have you enjoyed watching youngsters bloom from CoE, especially the U-19 players with whom you spend a considerable amount of time?

VVS Laxman with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

There has been a lot of focus on camps in the North East; can you elaborate?

How do they get more exposure?

How has the introduction of the U-15 category for women helped in identifying players?

When you switch roles from administrator to mentor coach, does it help that you see these players up close as an administrator?

When you look back at the almost five years of your journey at NCA/CoE, what’s the most satisfying aspect?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in December 2021. What began at a modest facility inside the M Chinnaswamy Stadium has since evolved into a much larger assignment, with Laxman now at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence, the state-of-the-art facility on the outskirts of the city.The Hyderabadi, whose playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience, is set to complete his tenure later this year.In an exclusive interview with TOI, Laxman reflects on his journey at the CoE, the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition, evolve and transform.ExcerptsIt has been a very fulfilling journey. When I started in late December 2021, we were working with a relatively small facility, and today we have a much larger and more comprehensive Centre of Excellence. The then BCCI secretary and current ICC chairman, Jay Shah, deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to invest in this facility and create an ecosystem of this scale. I am also grateful to the leadership for giving me the freedom and trust to develop and execute the vision we had for the CoE.For me, the biggest change is not just the infrastructure but also the ecosystem we have built around it, bringing together coaching, sports science, technology and education.This is extremely important to the BCCI. The CoE cannot be only for contracted players. If we want to strengthen Indian cricket, we have to strengthen the pathway beneath the international level as well.We are therefore trying to give domestic and pathway players greater access to quality coaching, sports science, performance analysis and technology. The idea is to identify potential early and give players the right environment to develop. Ultimately, CoE should contribute to the entire Indian cricket ecosystem, not just one particular group of players.It is a very encouraging trend. Players who have played at the first-class or international level have enormous knowledge and experience, and naturally many of them want to give something back to the game. But playing and coaching are two different skill sets. That is why coach education is important. We help them understand communication, planning, leadership and most importantly, how to transfer their experience to another player. More players are now recognising that their impact on the game can continue well beyond their playing careers.It’s not one session; it’s an ongoing mentoring process. Transition from player to coach doesn’t happen overnight. It is really a change in mindset. As a player, your primary responsibility is your own performance. As a coach, your responsibility is to make other people better. Through our coaching courses, we expose former and current players to communication, leadership, planning, managing different personalities and understanding individual players. The biggest learning is that coaching is not about showing people how much you know, but it is about helping the player discover how much they can achieve.The scale of our high performance work has grown significantly. Throughout the year, we run programmes across the pathway for both men and women players from the U-16, U-19, and U-23 age groups, as well as targeted specialist skill camps, including fast and spin bowler camps. We now directly support more than 150 players annually, and the impact is clear in the outcomes we are seeing: improved skill levels, stronger readiness for international cricket, and more players progressing successfully through the pathway into higher levels. Our objective is to create a continuous pathway from age group cricket right through to international level.It has been a very exciting process because women’s cricket in India has grown tremendously. The support ecosystem has to grow at the same pace. We are working on a more structured system around women’s cricket. We are also investing in developing coaches and support staff. Importantly, we don’t want to copy the men’s system. Women’s cricket has its own requirements, and we need to develop expertise around those specific needs.That is one of the most rewarding parts of my role. When you see a young player come into the CoE with potential and then watch him develop not just as a cricketer but also as a person, it gives you enormous satisfaction. With U-19 players, you are dealing with an important stage of their development. You are not just preparing them for the next tournament; you are trying to give them the habits, discipline, resilience, and awareness for a long career. When you subsequently see them progress into India A or senior cricket, it is incredibly satisfying.So with the under-19s or the A-teams, it's about getting better every day as a player in every aspect of their game. So it's not only about skill, but the mental aspect, the physical aspect, and how they can improve, because at the end of the day, any sport you play, any match you play, if you don't have that competitive spirit, then you're not a sports person.So you go out there to perform, you go out there to win the match and win the series, but at the same time, whether it's with under-19s or with the India players, it's also about measuring objectively how you're progressing after every match.It’s satisfying when you see that progress in a player because the whole endeavour is: Can they reach a stage where they can win matches for the senior Indian team in any international fixture and also perform at the highest level?The domestic circuit and structure is so robust, and there are so many matches happening across the different age groups. There's a lot of emphasis on developing the talent in the North-East.So we have camps which are dedicated to the North-East players, men and women from U-19 to senior age group. It’s great to see that every year the quality of those players has definitely gotten better, and the only way it will get better is if they get more exposure.By playing against good teams. You test yourself and gain confidence only when you play against good teams and do well; that's how they get exposure.We started it three years ago. It allows us to strengthen the bench and see players develop. We have players from the first batch who went on to play for India. G Kamalini was in the first batch of the U-15 tournament, and she played for India. So it's great to see not only the boys, but also the girls, benefiting from the various tournaments and camps we run under the BCCI umbrella.Coaching and mentoring come naturally because, as an India player, my interactions with the youngsters were always very seamless and holistic. You share your experiences, help them evolve and develop as cricketers, and maximise their potential.The administration part is obviously a different experience, and luckily again, the structures in the BCCI system made that seamless as well. The best part of this role is getting to see so many players come, perform, get selected, attend the camps, and repeat the process the next year.So it's great to see some of the players who were attending the U-19 camps in 2022 playing for India in 2025-26.The most satisfying thing has been seeing the ecosystem come together. It is not about one facility or one individual. It is about coaches, SSM professionals, performance analysts, grounds staff, administrators and players all working towards the same objective. I am particularly proud that the CoE has evolved into a place where players don’t come only when they are injured. They come to develop their skills, improve physically, learn and become better cricketers.The most fulfilling part of this journey as the CoE head of cricket has been seeing the players' transformation, and we hope they've now achieved their dream and will continue to bring laurels to the country.Ultimately, the real success will be when these systems continue to benefit Indian cricket for many years to come.
Article Summary: Vvs laxman has been at the helm of the bcci centre of excellence since december 2021. The hyderabadi's playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience. He is set to complete his tenure later this year. In an exclusive interview with toi, he reflects on his journey at the centre.

Article Title: Prasidh Krishna reveals his definition of aggression: 'It's about what I'm doing'

NEW DELHI: Every fast bowler has his own way of showing aggression. Some try to unsettle batters with eye contact, some stay calm, others rely on yorkers, constant appeals or words. India pacer Prasidh Krishna has a different approach - he believes his aggression is best shown through his bowling.Krishna credited disciplined bowling, strong fielding and an attacking mindset for India’s early success against Sri Lanka. The hosts were reduced to 8/2 before bad light ended Day Two of the second Test at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground on Monday. India had declared on 503/9 after centuries from Devdutt Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel.The bowlers had only a short window to work with, but Krishna made it count, picking up a wicket with just his second delivery of the second over.Krishna said aggression is not necessarily about showing emotion or getting into a verbal battle with the opposition.“Yeah, I would like to say so. I mean, aggression can come out in different ways, and for me it is about what I'm doing when I'm bowling. It's very easy for people to get away or be distracted by what's happening in the pitch.There's too much happening, there's not too much happening, but I think the focus is still to come in and bowl those areas with full effort,” Krishna told the broadcasters before the start of Day 3’s play.Krishna bowled back of a length outside off and found enough movement from the surface to trouble Lahiru Udara. The Sri Lankan opener edged towards gully, where Yashasvi Jaiswal completed an excellent diving catch to dismiss him for one.Krishna said the wicket was a result of both the conditions and Jaiswal’s fielding effort.“Yeah, I think it was, there’s something in the pitch, of course. Maybe stopped a little bit. There was a bit of seam, and I think credit goes to Jaiswal for the catch that he took. It was an exceptional one. We have been putting in some effort on the field in practice, so I think it just paid off,” he mentioned.India had very little time to bowl before bad light stopped play. Manav Suthar then dismissed Prabath Jayasuriya for two with the final delivery of the day, leaving Sri Lanka at 8/2.Krishna stressed that creating chances is only half the job and the fielders also need to complete the opportunity.“100%. I think 50% of the job is bowling the ball there, getting an edge, but 50% is taking it as well, and we have been pretty good at doing that. I think it's also doing the simple things right, which we have been doing well, and that's what shows,” he added.Krishna also spoke about the need to adjust his length according to the pitch. He said the Indian coaching and analysis staff work together to decide the right approach for each surface.“Length is something that keeps changing with pitches that we play on. So we sit with analysts, coaches, and everything and decide on what's the kind of length that we want to be bowling on different surfaces. And yeah, natural length was something that I could say when I was not playing for the country, but when I'm here I need to be bowling every length that the team wants, and I'm trying to do that,” he concluded.

The 2025-26 ABB FIA Formula E World Championship will end in London this weekend, with Rounds 16 and 17 taking place at Excel London on August 15 and 16. While the title battle is expected to be closely fought, sustainability will also be a major focus at the 2026 Hankook London E-Prix. The event is not only about the final two races of the Formula E season. Its sustainability efforts cover energy, waste, food packaging, community projects, education and opportunities for young people.As the championship reaches its season finale, the London E-Prix aims to show how electric racing can combine competition with efforts focused on sustainability and community impact.The London E-Prix will run on 100% certified renewable mains electricity, supported by solar power generated from Excel London’s eco-friendly extension. Track lighting and buffer zones will use dedicated battery storage systems. This will help eliminate the need for continuous generator use. Any remaining emissions will be fully offset.The event will follow a strict zero-waste-to-landfill policy. Non-hazardous waste will be sent for high-rate recycling. Surplus food waste will be composted on-site using commercial wormeries. Used cooking oil will be recycled into biofuel to power plant and machinery.Materials that cannot be recycled will be converted into clean energy.ID@undefinedCaption not available.Food concessions at the 2026 Hankook London E-Prix will use packaging from Notpla, a fellow B Corp-certified brand.The packaging is made from seaweed and natural plant extracts and is home-compostable. It will replace single-use plastics across catering operations and support a circular economy.Mobile provider giffgaff has joined Formula E as the championship's first-ever B Corp partner.The partnership will support the €25,000 Better Futures Fund initiative with Big Issue Recruit. It also includes trackside workshops during race week and aims to inspire young people to become future leaders in motorsport and sustainability.Formula E's Community Tour will give more than 380 local residents access to the event through two dedicated sessions.The programme brings together more than 15 community, diversity and youth organisations. It includes career-focused sessions for young adults and track tours for local charity beneficiaries, giving underrepresented groups behind-the-scenes access to electric racing.The FIA Girls on Track programme will return to London, with 150 young women aged 12 to 18 taking part.The programme will offer career panels, garage tours, simulator access and discussions on tackling online cyberbullying in sport. Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge

El Rubius reacted honestly after his elimination from MrBeast’s $1 million challenge, calling it “unfair” and claiming he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings. His response felt real and balanced, especially after MrBeast’s team later sent him a cake, softening the moment.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit







El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeast’s $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. But for a 25-year-old techie the craze for IPL tickets for RCB vs CSK turned too costly and he was duped for a massive Rs. 1.46 lakh.The techie, a resident of B Narayanapura, fell into a trap by a post posted by a fraudster who posed himself as a ticket seller on Instagram.As per a report in Deccan Herald, the techie alleged in a complaint to Mahadevapura Police that an individual claiming to be Sumit Biswal promised he could arrange IPL tickets along with food coupons.As per the techie, Biswal was introduced him as a senior supervisor for ticket counter at M Chinnaswamy Stadium"He asked me to come near the stadium gate number 10, saying someone would deliver the tickets within minutes, and even sent an email confirmation to gain my trust," the complainant told Deccan Herald."Initially, I agreed to buy two tickets for Rs 3,700 each,but he kept asking for more money under various pretexts such as refundable security deposits, additional ID cards and food coupons.Trusting him, I made multiple payments - even using my mother’s bank account after exhausting my own limits—and ended up transferring around Rs 1.46 lakh," he added.Bhuvneshwar Kumar’s incisive spell of 3-41, coming after a marauding batting show from Tim David, Rajat Patidar and Devdutt Padikkal, propelled Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) to a commanding 43-run victory over Chennai Super Kings (CSK) in their IPL 2026 encounter at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium on Sunday.The contest saw RCB’s batting unit dismantle CSK’s attack with relentless hitting, as David’s 70 not out off just 25 balls and Patidar’s unbeaten 48 off only 19 balls provided for the late fireworks after Padikkal’s fluent 50 off 29 balls had set the tone for the daunting total.Their combined effort lifted RCB to a daunting 250/3, thus setting a new record for highest total in IPL 2026. In reply, CSK faltered under scoreboard pressure, with Sarfaraz Khan’s 50 off 24 balls and Prashant Veer’s 43 the lone acts of resistance amid a string of failures from the top order.Bhuvneshwar was at his disciplined best and even crossed the 200-mark in terms of wickets in IPL, with others also chipping in as CSK were bowled out for 207 in 19.4 overs. The comprehensive win also meant RCB have registered four consecutive triumphs over CSK for the first time in the IPL’s history.
Article Summary: Royal challengers bengaluru (rcb) beat chennai super kings (csk) in ipl 2026 encounter at the m chinnaswamy stadium on sunday. Rcb register their second win over csk in the ipl. Tim david, rajat patidar and devdutt padikkal all scored half-centuries for rcb. Bhuvneshwar kumar took 3-41 to help rcb reach 250/3.
